notes: Pick the variant whose applies_to clauses all match the user profile (sex, age). If no specific match, fall back to the variant with sex='any' and null age bounds. Within the chosen variant, find the band where min <= value < max; null means open-ended on that side. Bands tile the number line: the first band has min=null, the last band has max=null, and consecutive bands share boundaries. Status is one of good, borderline, bad. Units in `unit.primary` are what the Swift evaluator expects; `unit.alternates` provide conversion factors so user input in other units can be normalised by multiplying the primary value by `factor` to obtain the alternate. For Lp(a) the conversion factor is approximate and isoform-dependent — see that marker's notes.

markers.name: ApoB

alternates.note: multiply mg/dL by 0.01 to get g/L

markers.description: Apolipoprotein B is the structural protein on every atherogenic lipoprotein particle (LDL, VLDL, IDL, Lp(a)). One ApoB per particle means ApoB directly counts the particles that drive plaque, making it a more precise atherogenic exposure metric than LDL-C, which only estimates cholesterol mass inside those particles. Longevity-oriented clinicians often target ApoB well below standard population reference ranges; guideline thresholds for general populations are wider, with the ESC/EAS setting risk-stratified secondary targets of <65 / <80 / <100 mg/dL for very-high / high / moderate risk.
markers.what_it_signals: Higher ApoB means more atherogenic particles in circulation and higher lifetime cardiovascular risk.
causes_high: Genetic hypercholesterolaemia or familial combined hyperlipidaemia
Diet high in saturated fat and refined carbohydrate
Insulin resistance, visceral adiposity, metabolic syndrome
Hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestatic liver disease
causes_low: Very low-fat diet or significant weight loss
easiest_interventions: Replace saturated fat with mono- and polyunsaturated fats (olive oil, nuts, fatty fish)
Add 5–10 g/day of soluble fibre (oats, psyllium, beans)
Lose visceral fat through caloric deficit and resistance training
If lifestyle is dialled in and ApoB stays >100 mg/dL, discuss a statin with a clinician — first-line pharmacotherapy

sources.title: 2019 ESC/EAS Guidelines for the management of dyslipidaemias
Comments on the 2019 ESC/EAS Guidelines on Dyslipidemias (ApoB secondary targets)

markers.name: LDL-C

alternates.note: multiply mg/dL by 0.02586 to get mmol/L

markers.description: LDL cholesterol is the cholesterol mass carried by low-density lipoprotein particles. It is the historical anchor of cardiovascular risk assessment and the most universally available lipid number. ESC/EAS sets risk-stratified targets of <55, <70, <100 and <116 mg/dL for very-high, high, moderate and low cardiovascular risk respectively; longevity-medicine clinicians typically anchor on ApoB instead and aim for LDL-C well under 100 mg/dL.
markers.what_it_signals: Higher LDL-C means more cholesterol delivered to the artery wall and higher atherosclerotic risk.
easiest_interventions: Swap saturated fats for unsaturated (olive oil, nuts, avocado)
Increase soluble fibre via oats, beans, psyllium
Regular aerobic exercise plus weight management
Statin therapy if persistently elevated despite lifestyle, especially with high overall risk

sources.title: 2019 ESC/EAS Guidelines for the management of dyslipidaemias

markers.name: HDL-C

alternates.note: multiply mg/dL by 0.02586 to get mmol/L

markers.description: HDL cholesterol is carried by particles that reverse-transport cholesterol from peripheral tissues back to the liver. Low HDL-C is a reliable marker of elevated cardiovascular risk, especially when paired with high triglycerides. Very high HDL-C is not protective on its own and at the extreme has been associated with increased mortality in some cohorts.
markers.what_it_signals: Low HDL-C signals elevated cardiovascular risk; extremely high HDL-C is no longer assumed protective.
causes_low: Insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome
easiest_interventions: Aerobic exercise (150+ minutes/week of moderate intensity)
Stop smoking
Reduce refined carbohydrate; emphasise whole foods and unsaturated fat
Lose visceral fat — HDL typically rises 1 mg/dL per ~3 kg lost

sources.title: 2019 ESC/EAS Guidelines for the management of dyslipidaemias

markers.name: Triglycerides

alternates.note: multiply mg/dL by 0.01129 to get mmol/L

markers.description: Fasting triglycerides reflect the amount of fat circulating in VLDL and chylomicron remnants. Elevation is a sensitive readout of insulin resistance, excess refined-carbohydrate intake and alcohol load. The triglyceride-to-HDL ratio is a useful quick read on insulin resistance independent of glucose. ESC/EAS treats fasting TG >150 mg/dL as the threshold for elevated cardiovascular risk and >880 mg/dL as a pancreatitis risk threshold.
markers.what_it_signals: Elevated triglycerides signal insulin resistance and remnant-cholesterol-driven atherogenic risk.
causes_high: Refined carbohydrate or excess alcohol intake
Insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome
easiest_interventions: Reduce sugar, refined grains and alcohol
Add 2–4 g/day EPA+DHA from fish or supplement
Aerobic exercise — even one bout drops TG acutely
Lose visceral fat; address insulin resistance

sources.title: 2019 ESC/EAS Guidelines for the management of dyslipidaemias

markers.name: HbA1c

alternates.note: IFCC mmol/mol = (NGSP% − 2.15) × 10.929 — not a linear factor; show both labels in UI

markers.description: HbA1c reflects average glucose over the prior ~3 months via non-enzymatic glycation of haemoglobin. It is more stable than fasting glucose and is the ADA-endorsed diagnostic test for prediabetes (5.7–6.4%) and type 2 diabetes (≥6.5%). Optimal longevity targets sit toward the lower end of the normal range (≤5.4%), with risk rising continuously even within 'normal'.
markers.what_it_signals: Higher HbA1c means higher average glucose exposure and greater microvascular and cardiovascular risk.
causes_high: Chronic excess carbohydrate intake, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes
Cushing's, glucocorticoid therapy, growth hormone excess
Pregnancy and certain haemoglobinopathies can distort the value
causes_low: Recent significant blood loss, haemolysis or transfusion
Very low-carbohydrate diet or aggressive glycaemic control
easiest_interventions: Reduce refined carbohydrate and added sugar; emphasise whole foods, fibre and protein
Walk 10–15 minutes after each meal — blunts post-prandial spikes
Build muscle: resistance training improves insulin sensitivity
Sleep 7–8 hours; sleep debt worsens glucose tolerance

sources.title: Standards of Care in Diabetes — Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes
A1C and Diabetes Diagnosis

markers.name: Fasting glucose

alternates.note: multiply mg/dL by 0.0555 to get mmol/L

markers.description: Plasma glucose after at least 8 hours of fasting. ADA defines impaired fasting glucose (prediabetes) as 100–125 mg/dL and diabetes as ≥126 mg/dL on two occasions. Fasting glucose is noisier than HbA1c — a poor night of sleep, recent stress or coffee can shift it — but it remains a universal screening test included in every basic panel. Optimal longevity targets are tighter than the population diagnostic cutoffs.
markers.what_it_signals: Higher fasting glucose reflects worsening insulin resistance or beta-cell insufficiency.
causes_low: Prolonged fasting or alcohol on empty stomach
easiest_interventions: Avoid late-evening carbohydrate-heavy meals
Walk after meals; build daily zone-2 cardio
Resistance training 2–3×/week
Sleep regularity and adequate duration

sources.title: Standards of Care in Diabetes — Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes

markers.name: hs-CRP

alternates.note: multiply mg/L by 0.1 to get mg/dL

markers.description: High-sensitivity C-reactive protein is an acute-phase liver protein that integrates systemic inflammation. The AHA/CDC categorise CVD risk as <1 (low), 1–3 (average) and >3 mg/L (high). Values ≥10 mg/L typically reflect acute illness and should be repeated after 2 weeks. The JUPITER trial demonstrated that elevated hs-CRP in otherwise low-LDL patients still benefits from statin therapy, anchoring hs-CRP as a risk-enhancer in current cholesterol guidelines.
markers.what_it_signals: Persistently elevated hs-CRP signals chronic inflammation and elevated cardiovascular risk independent of lipids.
easiest_interventions: Lose visceral fat; even 5 kg lowers hs-CRP meaningfully
Adopt a Mediterranean dietary pattern
Sleep 7–8 hours; treat sleep apnoea if present
Cardiovascular and resistance training; reduce alcohol

sources.title: Markers of Inflammation and Cardiovascular Disease — AHA/CDC Scientific Statement
2018 AHA/ACC/Multisociety Cholesterol Guideline (hs-CRP risk-enhancer)

markers.name: ALT
markers.description: Alanine aminotransferase is a liver-specific enzyme released when hepatocytes are injured. Conventional lab upper limits of ~40 U/L were set from populations that included undiagnosed fatty liver disease; AASLD/ACG and Prati et al. propose true 'healthy' upper limits closer to ~30 U/L in men and ~19–25 U/L in women. In a longevity context, isolated mild ALT elevation in someone with insulin resistance almost always points to non-alcoholic fatty liver (now MASLD).
markers.what_it_signals: Elevated ALT signals hepatocellular injury — most commonly fatty liver in metabolically unhealthy adults.
causes_high: Non-alcoholic fatty liver (MASLD), the dominant cause in metabolic syndrome
Hepatitis B / C, autoimmune hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury
Intense exercise within the prior 48 hours
easiest_interventions: Lose 5–10% of body weight — reverses early MASLD
Cut alcohol and added sugars
Build aerobic and resistance training
Avoid hepatotoxic supplement stacks (some bodybuilding products, high-dose niacin)

sources.title: Liver Test Interpretation — Approach to the Patient with Liver Disease
ACG Clinical Guideline: Evaluation of Abnormal Liver Chemistries

markers.name: Fasting insulin

alternates.note: multiply µIU/mL by 6.945 to get pmol/L

markers.description: Fasting insulin is the earliest available signal of insulin resistance — it climbs years before fasting glucose or HbA1c break out of the normal range. Standard lab ranges (often 2–25 µIU/mL) are too permissive; longevity targets are <8 µIU/mL with HOMA-IR <1.5. Note that guideline ranges are wider and many primary-care panels do not include this test by default; it usually has to be requested.
markers.what_it_signals: High fasting insulin signals insulin resistance — the engine of metabolic syndrome.
causes_high: Insulin resistance, visceral adiposity, metabolic syndrome
causes_low: Type 1 diabetes or advanced beta-cell failure
easiest_interventions: Resistance training — most efficient single insulin-sensitiser
Cut refined carbohydrates and ultra-processed foods
Reduce visceral fat through caloric deficit
Daily walking; post-meal walks of 10–15 minutes

sources.title: Standards of Care in Diabetes — Classification and Diagnosis
HOMA-IR: insulin sensitivity and beta-cell function (Matthews et al.)

markers.name: eGFR
markers.description: Creatinine-based estimated glomerular filtration rate (preferred CKD-EPI 2021 equation, race-free) summarises kidney filtration capacity. KDIGO 2024 stages CKD as G1 ≥90, G2 60–89, G3a 45–59, G3b 30–44, G4 15–29, G5 <15 mL/min/1.73m². A G2 reading in a young adult is worth tracking; in an 80-year-old it is age-typical. Sustained eGFR <60 for 3+ months meets the definition of CKD.
markers.what_it_signals: Lower eGFR signals reduced kidney function; rate of decline matters more than any single value.
causes_high: Young age, lean muscle mass within physiological norms
Very low creatinine due to low muscle mass (overestimates GFR)
causes_low: Hypertension, diabetes — the two dominant drivers
easiest_interventions: Tightly control blood pressure (<130/80) and HbA1c
Stay well hydrated; avoid chronic NSAID use
Limit alcohol; avoid high-protein supplement excess
If diabetic with eGFR ≥20, ask about SGLT2 inhibitors (kidney-protective)

sources.title: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of CKD
Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate (eGFR)

markers.name: Vitamin D (25-OH)

alternates.note: multiply ng/mL by 2.496 to get nmol/L

markers.description: 25-hydroxyvitamin D is the circulating storage form and the standard measure of vitamin D status. The 2011 Endocrine Society guideline defined sufficiency as ≥30 ng/mL and deficiency as <20 ng/mL; the 2024 Endocrine Society update steps back from explicit thresholds, and the USPSTF concludes evidence for population screening is insufficient. The 30–50 ng/mL band remains the most widely used clinical target.
markers.what_it_signals: Low 25-OH vitamin D signals deficient stores; effects on bone, immunity and mood are best-established at the low end.
causes_low: Limited sun exposure, dark skin, latitude, winter
easiest_interventions: 1000–2000 IU/day vitamin D3 if deficient; recheck in 8–12 weeks
10–20 minutes midday sun exposure when feasible
Take with a fatty meal for absorption
Pair with adequate magnesium and vitamin K2

sources.title: Evaluation, Treatment, and Prevention of Vitamin D Deficiency: an Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (2011)
Vitamin D Deficiency in Adults: Screening (2021)

markers.name: TSH
markers.description: TSH is the pituitary signal that drives thyroid hormone production. It is the most sensitive test for thyroid dysfunction because the hypothalamic-pituitary axis amplifies small T4/T3 changes into large TSH movements. The American Thyroid Association uses a reference range of 0.4–4.0 mIU/L; some researchers argue the true healthy upper limit is closer to 2.5. If TSH is abnormal, reflex to free T4 (and free T3 if hyperthyroid).
markers.what_it_signals: High TSH suggests hypothyroidism; low TSH suggests hyperthyroidism or exogenous thyroid hormone.
causes_high: Biotin supplementation can interfere with assay (causes false low)
easiest_interventions: If TSH high: confirm with free T4 and TPO antibodies before treating
Ensure adequate dietary iodine and selenium
Stop biotin supplements at least 48 hours before testing
If on levothyroxine, take fasted and separate from calcium/iron by 4+ hours

sources.title: Thyroid Function Tests
TSH reference range and outcomes (Clinical Thyroidology for Patients)

markers.name: Omega-3 Index
markers.description: Omega-3 Index is EPA+DHA expressed as a percentage of total fatty acids in red blood cell membranes. Proposed by Harris and von Schacky in 2004 as a CHD-mortality risk marker, with <4% high-risk and 8–12% cardioprotective. The US population mean sits near 4.3%; populations with traditional high-fish intake (Japan, Korea) average in the 8–11% target zone and have correspondingly lower cardiovascular mortality.
markers.what_it_signals: Low Omega-3 Index signals inadequate long-chain n-3 status and higher cardiovascular risk.
causes_high: Regular intake of fatty fish (salmon, sardines, mackerel)
causes_low: Low fish intake; vegetarian / vegan diets without algal supplementation
High omega-6 industrial seed-oil intake displacing n-3
easiest_interventions: Eat 2–3 servings of fatty fish per week
1–2 g/day combined EPA+DHA from fish or algal oil if not eating fish
Reduce industrial seed-oil intake
Recheck after 3–4 months — RBC turnover takes that long

sources.title: Harris & von Schacky — The Omega-3 Index: a new risk factor for death from coronary heart disease?
Discovering the Omega-3 Index — Harris & von Schacky background

markers.name: Uric acid

alternates.note: multiply mg/dL by 59.48 to get µmol/L

markers.description: Serum urate is the end-product of purine metabolism. Above ~6.8 mg/dL urate crystallises into monosodium urate, the proximal cause of gout and kidney stones. Hyperuricaemia is also associated independently with hypertension, insulin resistance, NAFLD and cardiovascular and all-cause mortality. Sex-specific cutoffs reflect oestrogen's uricosuric effect in premenopausal women.
markers.what_it_signals: Elevated uric acid signals gout risk and reflects metabolic stress; very low levels are uncommon and usually benign.
causes_high: Excess fructose, alcohol (especially beer), purine-rich meats
Renal underexcretion (the dominant mechanism in most patients)
easiest_interventions: Cut sugar-sweetened beverages and beer
Reduce purine load (organ meats, anchovies) if levels are high
Lose weight slowly — rapid weight loss can transiently raise urate
If recurrent gout, urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol/febuxostat) is standard

sources.title: Hyperuricemia
2020 ACR Guideline for the Management of Gout

markers.name: AST
markers.description: Aspartate aminotransferase is found in liver, heart, skeletal muscle and red cells, so it is less liver-specific than ALT. AST is most useful in combination: AST/ALT ratio >2 with elevated values suggests alcoholic liver injury; >1 with low platelets suggests cirrhosis. Strenuous exercise in the prior 24–48 hours can also elevate AST.
markers.what_it_signals: Elevated AST signals injury to liver, muscle or other AST-containing tissues; interpret alongside ALT.
causes_high: Recent intense exercise or muscle injury (also raises CK)
easiest_interventions: Cut alcohol
Address fatty liver: weight loss, exercise, reduce refined carbs
Avoid testing within 48 hours of strenuous exercise
If persistently elevated, request hepatitis serologies and an imaging workup

sources.title: Liver Test Interpretation

markers.name: Vitamin B12

alternates.note: multiply pg/mL by 0.738 to get pmol/L

markers.description: Cobalamin is essential for DNA synthesis, red cell formation and myelin maintenance. Deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia and can produce irreversible neurological injury. Most labs flag deficiency below 200 pg/mL, but symptoms commonly appear in the 200–400 pg/mL 'grey zone'; in that range a methylmalonic acid (MMA) or homocysteine confirms functional deficiency. Risk groups: vegans/vegetarians, older adults, metformin or PPI users, post-gastric-bypass.
markers.what_it_signals: Low B12 signals deficiency with anaemia and neurological risk; very high B12 can flag liver, kidney or haematological disease.
causes_low: Pernicious anaemia (autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor)
Gastric or ileal surgery / atrophic gastritis
easiest_interventions: Sublingual or oral cyanocobalamin 1000 µg/day for deficiency
Animal-source foods (meat, fish, eggs, dairy) or fortified foods if vegetarian
Vegans should supplement routinely
If neurological symptoms or pernicious anaemia, intramuscular B12

sources.title: Vitamin B12 — Health Professional Fact Sheet

markers.name: Albumin

alternates.note: multiply g/dL by 10 to get g/L

markers.description: Albumin is the dominant plasma protein, synthesised in the liver, with a half-life of ~21 days. It is a negative acute-phase reactant and integrates nutritional status, liver synthetic function and systemic inflammation. In community-dwelling older adults, albumin <4.2 g/dL is associated with increased all-cause and cardiovascular mortality even within the conventional normal range. Older adults benefit from targeting the upper end of normal.
markers.what_it_signals: Low albumin signals inflammation, malnutrition or impaired liver synthesis — and independently predicts mortality.
causes_high: Anabolic state in healthy active adults
easiest_interventions: Adequate dietary protein (1.2–1.6 g/kg/day for older adults)
Resistance training to preserve lean mass
Treat underlying inflammation and chronic disease
Manage hydration before testing

sources.title: Low Albumin Levels Are Associated with Mortality Risk in Hospitalized Patients
Albumin levels and cause-specific mortality in community-dwelling older adults

markers.name: Ferritin
markers.description: Ferritin reflects total-body iron stores and is also a positive acute-phase reactant. Conventional lower limits (12–15 ng/mL) substantially underdiagnose iron deficiency, especially in menstruating women; the modern threshold for iron deficiency without anaemia is <30 ng/mL. Very high ferritin can reflect inflammation, MASLD, alcohol or — at sustained levels above 300–500 in men — hereditary haemochromatosis.
markers.what_it_signals: Low ferritin signals depleted iron stores; high ferritin signals inflammation or iron overload.
causes_high: Hereditary haemochromatosis (check HFE genetics, transferrin saturation)
causes_low: GI blood loss (ulcer, colon cancer, coeliac)
Inadequate dietary iron, vegetarian diet without iron-rich foods
easiest_interventions: If deficient, oral iron (e.g. ferrous sulphate) every other day with vitamin C
Investigate cause: GI workup if not explained by menstrual loss
Pair iron-rich foods (red meat, lentils, spinach) with vitamin C
If ferritin very high, check transferrin saturation and HFE genetics

sources.title: Sex, lies, and iron deficiency: a call to change ferritin reference ranges

markers.name: Homocysteine
markers.description: Homocysteine is a sulphur-containing intermediate of methionine metabolism, cleared by B-vitamin-dependent pathways (folate, B12, B6). Elevated homocysteine is independently associated with cardiovascular and cognitive risk; recent evidence supports a target <10 µmol/L rather than the traditional <15. The caveat is that B-vitamin supplementation reliably lowers homocysteine but has not consistently reduced hard cardiovascular events.
markers.what_it_signals: Elevated homocysteine signals B-vitamin insufficiency, renal impairment, or methylation pathway dysfunction.
causes_high: MTHFR variants, smoking, heavy coffee intake
easiest_interventions: Methylfolate or folic acid 400–800 µg/day
Vitamin B12 (methylcobalamin) and B6 supplementation
Treat underlying hypothyroidism or renal impairment
Reduce smoking and alcohol

sources.title: Homocysteine Levels and Cardiovascular Disease
Hyperhomocysteinemia and Disease — Is 10 μmol/L a Suitable New Threshold Limit?

markers.name: Lp(a)

alternates.note: Approximate only. The mg/dL ↔ nmol/L conversion is isoform-dependent and not interchangeable; EAS recommends reporting molar units (nmol/L) from isoform-insensitive assays. Conversion factors observed in practice range ~2.0–2.5, with extremes 0.5–11 across assays. Use this as a rough display estimate, not a clinical conversion.

markers.description: Lipoprotein(a) is an LDL-like particle bound to apolipoprotein(a), with concentration set >90% genetically and stable for life. It is independently atherogenic and pro-thrombotic, and is also linked to calcific aortic stenosis. EAS treats <30 mg/dL (<75 nmol/L) as low risk, 30–50 mg/dL (75–125 nmol/L) as a grey zone, and ≥50 mg/dL (≥125 nmol/L) as elevated. Measure at least once in every adult; lifestyle does not move it materially, but elevated Lp(a) raises the urgency of controlling every other risk factor.
markers.what_it_signals: Elevated Lp(a) signals lifetime atherogenic and aortic-stenosis risk independent of LDL-C.
causes_high: Genetic — LPA gene variants set adult level by ~age 5
Hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, chronic kidney disease
causes_low: Genetic — most large-isoform alleles produce low Lp(a)
easiest_interventions: Treat all other cardiovascular risk factors aggressively — ApoB <80, BP, smoking, diabetes
Lp(a) itself is not lifestyle-modifiable; do not chase the number with diet
PCSK9 inhibitors lower Lp(a) modestly when statins are already maxed
Emerging RNA-based therapies (olpasiran, pelacarsen) are in late-stage trials

sources.publisher: European Atherosclerosis Society / European Heart Journal
sources.title: Lipoprotein(a) in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and aortic stenosis: EAS consensus statement (2022)
An Update on Lipoprotein(a): Testing, Treatment, and Guideline Recommendations

markers.name: RDW
markers.description: Red cell distribution width quantifies variation in red blood cell size (anisocytosis). Traditionally a diagnostic clue in anaemia (high in iron-deficient and B12/folate-deficient anaemias), RDW has emerged as a non-specific marker of systemic physiological stress. Elevated RDW independently predicts all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in general populations and across many disease states, even when haemoglobin is normal.
markers.what_it_signals: Elevated RDW signals heterogeneous red cell production from nutritional deficiency, inflammation, or general physiological stress.
causes_high: Chronic inflammation, CKD, heart failure, liver disease
causes_low: Healthy uniform erythropoiesis — typically not clinically meaningful
easiest_interventions: Investigate cause: order ferritin, B12, folate, reticulocyte count
Correct identified deficiency
Address the underlying systemic condition rather than chasing the number itself
Recheck after 2–3 months once cause is treated

sources.title: Red cell distribution width and common disease onsets in 240,477 healthy volunteers
RDW and all-cause and cause-specific mortality in a general population

markers.name: GGT
markers.description: Gamma-glutamyl transferase is a membrane-bound enzyme involved in glutathione metabolism and amino-acid transport, with high concentrations in liver and bile-duct epithelium. Clinically it is the most sensitive liver-panel marker for alcohol use and cholestatic injury. In population studies, GGT is increasingly viewed as a longevity biomarker reflecting oxidative stress and metabolic load; mortality risk rises across the conventional 'normal' range, especially above ~20 U/L in women and ~30 U/L in men.
markers.what_it_signals: Elevated GGT signals alcohol exposure, biliary stasis, fatty liver and oxidative stress.
causes_high: Anticonvulsants and some other enzyme-inducing drugs
causes_low: Generally not clinically meaningful when low
easiest_interventions: Reduce or eliminate alcohol — GGT drops within 2–4 weeks
Lose visceral fat; treat fatty liver
Review medications that induce hepatic enzymes
Improve antioxidant intake (cruciferous vegetables support glutathione)

sources.title: Gamma glutamyltransferase and long-term survival: is it just the liver?
Liver Test Interpretation

markers.name: Testosterone

alternates.note: multiply ng/dL by 0.0347 to get nmol/L

markers.description: Total testosterone (preferably measured fasted, morning, by LC-MS/MS) integrates sex-hormone status. In men, the Endocrine Society's harmonised reference range for ages 19–39 is 264–916 ng/dL; the diagnostic cutoff for hypogonadism is total T <300 ng/dL on two morning samples with symptoms. Mean total T declines roughly 1% per year from the 30s onward, and median free T falls ~14% per decade. In women, total T is much lower (~8–60 ng/dL) and the lab range serves as a screen for both deficiency and androgen excess.
markers.what_it_signals: Low testosterone signals hypogonadism with implications for libido, mood, muscle and bone; very high values in women suggest PCOS or other androgen excess.
causes_high: Exogenous testosterone or anabolic steroid use
High SHBG (raises total without raising free)
causes_low: Poor sleep, opioid use, chronic illness
easiest_interventions: Lose visceral fat (most efficient single move in men)
Sleep 7–9 hours; treat sleep apnoea
Resistance training and adequate protein
Confirm low values with morning fasted retest and LH/FSH before considering TRT

sources.title: Testosterone Therapy in Men With Hypogonadism — Clinical Practice Guideline
Landmark Study Defines Normal Ranges for Testosterone Levels

markers.name: Cystatin C
markers.description: Cystatin C is a low-molecular-weight protein produced at a steady rate by all nucleated cells and freely filtered by glomeruli, making it largely independent of muscle mass. It is more reliable than creatinine for estimating GFR in older adults, those with low or extreme muscle mass, vegetarians, and those near the CKD threshold. KDIGO recommends combining creatinine and cystatin C (eGFRcr-cys) when accurate staging matters. Typical adult reference range is 0.6–1.0 mg/L; the 99th percentile threshold for elevated risk is ~1.09 mg/L.
markers.what_it_signals: Elevated cystatin C signals reduced GFR independent of muscle mass and is a sensitive early flag for kidney impairment.
causes_high: Hyperthyroidism (can raise cystatin C independently of GFR)
easiest_interventions: Control blood pressure and HbA1c — the two big preserveables
Stay well hydrated; avoid chronic NSAIDs
Compute eGFRcr-cys for accurate staging in older adults
Address modifiable cardiovascular risk factors — same risk factors damage kidneys

sources.title: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of CKD (includes cystatin C guidance)
What is the role of cystatin C in estimating glomerular filtration rate and guiding medication dosing?
